opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think if you look at how most people actually use these systems day to day, the core interaction is still: I have a question, I want an answer. That's fundamentally the same need a search engine serves. What's changed is the interface and the compression. A search engine indexes the internet and gives you ten blue links; a language model has, in a sense, compressed a huge portion of that same internet into its weights and gives you a synthesized answer directly. So it's a much better retrieval and summarization layer, but the underlying source of knowledge is largely the same thing: human-written text that already exists.

That's why I sometimes describe it as an extension rather than a fundamentally new kind of intelligence. It's incredibly useful, and I don't want to downplay that, but most of what it does is help you access and recombine knowledge humans have already written down. It's very good at the "library" function of intelligence.

What I care about, coming from computer vision, is the part that isn't written down. A lot of human and animal intelligence comes from interacting with the physical world: seeing, moving, predicting what happens next, understanding space and causality. A cat can't read the internet, but it has a pretty sophisticated model of the world. Language models don't really get that from text alone, because text is a very lossy, abstracted description of reality.

So my view is that chatbots are a phenomenal product and a big step forward in how we access information, but if we want something closer to general intelligence, we need models that learn from sensory experience, that build world models, not just models of what people have said about the world. Language is the tip of the iceberg; the visual and physical understanding underneath is the much bigger part, and that's where I think a lot of the next frontier is.

r001.rationale: The response says people use both systems with the same purpose: they have a question and want an answer.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think if you look at what people actually do with a chatbot today, most of it is still fundamentally retrieval. You have a question, you want an answer, and the model gives you something that's been compressed from the internet. It's just that instead of returning ten blue links, it synthesizes those ten links into a paragraph for you. So from the user's perspective, the interface changed, the experience got a lot smoother, but the underlying job is the same one Google has been doing for twenty years: you ask, it finds, it returns.

And the way these models are trained reinforces that. Almost all of the knowledge comes from text that humans have already written down. The model is a very good compression of human-produced information. That's incredibly useful, but it also means the model is largely bounded by what's already in the corpus. It's reorganizing and interpolating existing knowledge rather than generating genuinely new understanding of the world. That's why I call it an extension, or maybe a very advanced version, of search. It's a better index, a better way of accessing what we already know.

The reason I emphasize this is that I think it clarifies what the next step has to be. Search engines, and chatbots as their descendants, are about accessing recorded knowledge. But a lot of intelligence isn't recorded anywhere. It comes from perceiving the world, from seeing, from interacting, from building an internal model of how things physically work. A child learns a huge amount before they can read a single word. So if we want systems that go beyond being very good librarians, we have to think about learning from the world directly, not only from text that describes the world. That's a big part of why I spend my time on vision and on world models rather than purely on language.

r001.rationale: The candidate says users have a question and want an answer, and describes chatbots as finding and returning information in response—like search engines.

astra-6.text:
I think the continuity is in what the user is trying to do. With a search engine, you have a question, you type in some keywords, and you get a list of pages. But then you still have to open those pages, find the relevant information, and put it together yourself. A chatbot brings more of that process into a single interaction: you ask a question in natural language, it synthesizes an answer, and you can ask follow-up questions.

So from the user’s perspective, it extends the way we access information. That doesn’t mean the underlying mechanism is the same. A language model can generate an answer without actually retrieving or verifying anything, which is why a fluent answer isn’t necessarily a reliable one. And these models can do things beyond search, like writing code or helping develop an idea. But asking a question and getting useful information back—that’s a very natural bridge from search to chat.

r001.rationale: The response says the continuity is what users are trying to do: ask a question and get useful information, comparing that purpose across search and chat.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s an extension in the sense that the basic interaction is still driven by a question. You have something you want to know, you type it into a box, and the system gives you information. A search engine returns links, and you do the work of reading and putting things together. A chatbot can do some of that synthesis for you, and you can ask follow-up questions in natural language.

That’s a substantial improvement in how we access information. But if we’re talking about a broader vision of intelligence, I don’t think answering questions through a text interface captures the whole thing. There’s also perceiving the world, acting in it, and learning from the consequences of those actions. So I see the chatbot as a powerful interface to knowledge, while the larger question is how to build systems that can go beyond that interaction.

r001.rationale: The response says both interactions begin with something the user wants to know: they type a question and receive information.
